label: explain2-track-3
one_line: We make one prediction before looking: a simple cell-shape rule, locked in advance, can predict which kidney-cell balls have a dented hollow.
what: Our one main prediction: a simple model that knows only how many cells a ball has will predict the dents in its hollow better than plain guesses can. Many organs have a hollow space inside, called a lumen. Dog kidney cells grown in a gel form tiny balls with one such hollow. These cells are called MDCK cells (short for Madin-Darby canine kidney). You might expect the hollow to be round, like a water balloon. In fact it is often dented. A 2021 study offered a simple idea. Each cell brings a fixed length of inner wall. So the number of cells shapes the dents. We run no new lab work. We take that study's public measurements and public computer model. We tune the model on normal cells only. Then we lock the settings and check them on cells it has not seen. It must beat plain guesses. Two plain guesses are "always round" and "use the average".
why: Faulty hollow spaces are tied to kidney and other disease. A popular idea says fluid pressure puffs the hollow into a smooth balloon. The 2021 study suggests pressure may matter less than cell number and inner wall per cell. Other labs disagree, so the question is still open. We write our prediction down first. That is a fair way to make progress. We claim no cure and no medical effect.

steps.text: Download the public measurements from the 2021 paper. Save a fingerprint of each file. A fingerprint is a short code computed from the file. If anyone changed the file, the code would change.
steps.picture: Like keeping a receipt and noting its total.

steps.text: Recompute the numbers that earlier helpers quoted. The ones we checked matched. We did not redo them all.
steps.picture: Like adding up a shopping bill a second time.

steps.text: Fit a simple line on normal cells only. The line links the number of cells to how dented the hollow is.
steps.picture: Like drawing a trend line through test scores from one school.

steps.text: Lock the model's settings in a dated file. We do this before we look at the other cell types. The model has dials, such as how hard the fluid pushes and how long each cell's inner wall is. We call these settings.
steps.picture: Like sealing your exam answers in an envelope.

steps.text: Compare the model with plain guesses. The guesses are: always round, the average, and a line based on ball size alone. The size-only line is the hardest to beat, so it is our main yardstick.
steps.picture: Like asking whether a weather expert beats saying tomorrow will match today.

steps.text: Score the sealed answers on cells the model has not seen. The test is only partly blind. The 2021 authors adjusted two settings to fit their data. We also saw the group averages.
steps.picture: Like opening the envelope when a few hints have already leaked.

steps.text: Split the data by photo day, which is the day a set of cells was imaged. Each cell type was imaged on different days. So we cannot tell a cell-type difference from a day difference. To be fair, we hold out one whole day at a time and test on it.
steps.picture: Like comparing marks from two schools in two different years.

steps.text: Report the result in plain words. We report it whether the model wins or loses.
steps.picture: Like posting the score even when your team lost.

wrong_if: Our written bet is this. The locked model will beat the size-only line on normal cells from a day it never saw. If it does not, we were wrong. We were also wrong if it cannot beat "always round" or "the average" on cells it has not seen. We have not yet scored the locked model on unseen cells. This page describes the plan, not a result.
could_go_wrong: Each cell type was photographed on different days. So day-to-day noise could hide a real difference between cell types.

Normal cells already differ from day to day. The typical gap between days is about 0.07 on a scale from 0 to 1. That is like 7 points on a 100-point test. Some of the differences we hoped to detect are smaller than that. About a third of the left-over variation comes from which day the photo was taken.
The 2021 authors tuned two settings of their model on the same data. So our test is only partly blind.
The authors' own code did not run as published. Our patched run did not clearly match their results.

The 2021 authors ran their model many times with different settings, 243 in our check. We call this the published sweep. Even the best run fit normal cells worse than the plain average does. So our first check, which asks us to reproduce their model, may fail. We treat that as an expected warning, not a verdict.
We planned six tests of the model. Two of them lack enough data, so we may drop them. One has only 15 balls. The other needs another lab's images, and only a few example images are online.
One formula in our plan was written upside down. We found the correct version and it matches to 14 decimal places. We must fix the plan before we start.
We keep a list of rules that a computer has checked, using a tool called Lean. That list has no rule about lumen shape. So no proof tool backs the biology here.

questions.q: How do you know the lumens are dented?
questions.a: The 2021 paper measured it. Roundness was about 0.3 to 0.7 on a scale where 1 is a perfect ball. Between 10 and over 50 percent of the inner surface curved inward.

questions.q: How do you know the numbers are right?
questions.a: We re-ran scripts on the public files and got the quoted values. Each check was done by hand or script from the same files. We did not redo every number.
We did not rerun the Lean proofs. We did not measure pressure ourselves. We also did not confirm the authors' simulation settings.
No. The model still includes pressure. Another lab measured about 65 pascals in these balls and says pressure matters more. We do not know who is right.

questions.q: What result did the model get on unseen cells?
questions.a: None yet. We have not scored it. So far we have only checked the plain size-only line on normal cells. We left out one photo day at a time and tested on it. The typical error was 0.1214 for the size-only line and 0.1396 for the plain average. Lower is better, so the line wins. The gap is small: about 0.018 on a scale of 0 to 1.

questions.q: Why not just run a new experiment?
questions.a: That would cost far more. Public data lets us run a fair first test cheaply.
The locked model fails if it does no better than the size-only line, or than simple guesses, on unseen cells. We would report that.

questions.q: What are the six planned tests?
questions.a: We named them P1 to P6. P1 checks that we can reproduce the published model. P2 checks that the inner wall length per cell stays the same as cell count changes. P3 asks whether the model beats the size-only line on cells missing a protein called Rab11a. P4 asks whether it transfers to cells missing the tight-junction protein claudin. P5 asks whether it works on bigger balls. P6 asks whether it works on another lab's images. P5 and P6 may be dropped for lack of data.
P5 has only 15 balls. P6 has only example images online. We would need to ask the authors for more.

questions.q: Does this say anything about medicine?
questions.a: No. It tests an idea about shape in lab-grown cells only.

glossary.plain: The hollow space inside a tube or ball of cells.
A standard type of lab-grown cell from a dog's kidney. It forms small hollow balls.
A sheet of cells that lines a surface or a hollow, like the lining of a tube.
A tiny ball of lab-grown cells that copies a small part of an organ.
The push of fluid against the wall of a space.
The push of still fluid, such as water, against the walls that hold it.
A unit of pressure. 65 pascals is a very small push, far less than a tyre holds.
A set of simple rules run on a computer to mimic something real.
The adjustable numbers in a model, such as pressure or wall length. Tuning them means adjusting them until the model fits the data.
Numbers fixed and dated before we look at new data.
The 2021 authors' many runs of their model with different settings. We checked 243 of them.
Having parts of the wall that curve inward.
A score where 1 means perfectly smooth and round.
The face of each cell that points into the hollow.
A straight line drawn through points to show their overall pattern.
A trend line that predicts dentedness from ball size alone.
Cells whose results we keep hidden until the settings are locked.
The day a set of cells was imaged.
Hide one day's photos, fit on the other days, then test on the hidden day. Repeat for each day.
The typical size of a miss between a guess and the real value. Lower is better.
A statistical test of whether groups, such as photo days, differ by more than chance. Our result, p = 0.0025, means that chance alone would rarely give such a gap.
The share of variation that comes from which group a measurement belongs to. Ours is 0.355, so about a third of the variation comes from the photo day.
A short code computed from a file. Any change to the file changes the code.
Maths arguments that a computer has checked step by step.
Our list of rules that a computer has checked with Lean.
A computer run that imitates a real process.
The raw tables a paper shares so others can check it.

check_yourself.what: Open the 2021 paper and read the lumen shape results.
check_yourself.expect: A paper on lumen shape in dog kidney cell balls, open access.

check_yourself.what: Open the independent lab data record.
check_yourself.expect: Three files. The example images file is 7467521 bytes.

check_yourself.what: Fingerprint the downloaded source data zip. The code should match the one we recorded.
Recompute the day-to-day spread check. ANOVA is a test of whether days differ. ICC is the share of variation due to the day.
check_yourself.command: python an_power.py (in the t3-lumen-crit scripts folder)

check_yourself.what: Hide one photo day at a time and compare the size-only line with the plain average. The script prints the typical error for each. 'const' is the plain average. 'line' is the size-only line. Lower is better.
check_yourself.command: python an_loso.py (in the t3-lumen-crit scripts folder)

Notochord data 'cannot be a bounded-cost companion': a judgment, so not stated as fact.
Claim that all data-side numbers match 'exactly': the verifier called it too strong, so I said 'the ones we checked'.
Prediction that the published-sweep reproduction gate will fail: a forecast, not a sourced fact. The text says only that it may fail.
Need for an old NumPy and the authors' initial conditions: the agent's inference, not confirmed.
'Circular test' conclusion about identities: a judgment, so left out.
Advice to drop two tests and make two exploratory: a judgment; I said only that they may be dropped.
Cell-geometry and Thompson-library Lean theorems in the older copy: not opened by the verifier.
